pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Body Parts & Senses

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y1 'Animals, including humans'):** 'identify, name, draw and label the basic parts of the human body and say which part of the body is associated with each sense.' Two jobs: NAME/LABEL external body parts, and ASSOCIATE each of the five senses with its body part.

- **Standards — US (NGSS K-2):** no direct sense-organ PE (senses appear via 1-LS1-1, animals use body parts to sense and respond); this is chiefly a UK Y1 naming task, with the sense→organ mapping widely taught in early US science.

- **Operational details:** At 5–6 this is foundational NAMING plus a simple mapping: sight–eyes, hearing–ears, smell–nose, taste–tongue/mouth, touch–skin. Anchor each sense to a concrete first-hand experience ('use your nose to smell the orange') so the organ–sense link is felt, not memorised. Use the child's OWN body as the manipulative — point, label, act it out. Teach body-part vocabulary (head, arm, leg, hand, foot, etc.) alongside the sense organs. Two subtleties to handle gently: taste is the tongue (not the whole mouth) and touch is the skin (all over, not just fingertips). Keep it observational and celebratory of the body; no internal organs or mechanisms yet. This underpins later sense–brain–response modelling.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). The child labels basic external body parts on an outline and correctly matches each of the five senses to its body part, giving a real example for each ('I hear with my ears').
bestPractices: Anchor every sense to a first-hand sensory experience (smell an orange, feel textures, listen to sounds) so the organ–sense link is embodied, not rote.
Use the child's OWN body as the manipulative — point to, name and act out each part and sense.
Teach body-part names and sense organs together, building core vocabulary on a labelled body outline.
Clarify the two commonly-blurred mappings: taste = tongue (not the whole mouth), touch = skin (all over the body).
Keep it external and observational — no internal organs or mechanisms at this age; celebrate what the body can do.
Use multi-sensory sorting ('which sense tells you about this?') to apply the mapping to real objects.
keyRepresentations: A labelled body outline (head, arms, legs, hands, feet + eyes, ears, nose, tongue, skin).
A sense–organ matching set (eye–sight, ear–hearing, nose–smell, tongue–taste, skin–touch).
Real objects/experiences tagged by the sense that detects them (a bell–hearing, a flower–smell).
Icon pairs linking each sense symbol to its body part.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking we taste with the whole mouth rather than the tongue.
Thinking touch is only in the hands/fingers, not the skin all over the body.
Confusing smell and taste (they work together when eating).
Assuming eyes 'send out' something to see, rather than receiving light (an early seeing misconception — keep simple).
Muddling which organ goes with which sense (e.g. ears for smell).
Overlooking that other animals have these senses too (thinking senses are human-only).

learn.summary: For 5–6 year olds learning body parts and the five senses (UK Y1 'Animals, including humans'): name and label external body parts, and match each sense to its organ (sight–eyes, hearing–ears, smell–nose, taste–tongue, touch–skin). A strong approach anchors every sense to a first-hand sensory experience using the child's own body, then uses a labelled body figure and sorting activities to consolidate. Keep it external and observational — no internal organs or mechanisms yet.

activities.title: All about my body: label and reveal
feedback: When a child says 'I taste with my whole mouth', gently build on it: 'Your tongue does most of the tasting — put a tiny raisin on your tongue and notice the taste'.
When a child says only fingers feel, have them close their eyes while you (safely) stroke their arm or cheek: 'You felt that — your skin all over your body can feel'.
Celebrate correct matches with the child's own example: 'Yes! You smell the flower with your nose'.
If a child muddles ears/nose or similar, re-anchor with a real object: ring a bell ('which part hears it?').
activities.rationale: At 5–6 this is foundational naming plus a simple sense→organ mapping. Using the child's own body as the manipulative and attaching a vivid, doable example to each organ is intended to make the link felt rather than memorised. A labelled figure with reveal-on-tap names parts and models the organ→sense pairing; a lift-the-flap correction and whole-skin shimmer address the two commonly blurred mappings directly.
sourceClaims: DfE Y1 statutory: 'identify, name, draw and label the basic parts of the human body and say which part of the body is associated with each sense'.
Young children commonly think touch is only in the fingers and taste is in the whole mouth; anchoring senses to first-hand experiences supports accurate organ–sense mapping.
learnerActions: Look at a friendly child figure and point to each body part on your OWN body as it is named: head, arm, leg, hand, foot.
Say the name of each part aloud as you touch it.
Match each sense to its body part by touching or labelling: eyes for sight, ears for hearing, nose for smell, tongue for taste, skin for touch.
Give a real example out loud for each sense, e.g. 'I see with my eyes', 'I hear with my ears'.
Answer a lift-the-flap style question: 'What do you taste with?' — mainly your tongue.
Touch anywhere on your skin — an arm, a cheek — and say 'My skin feels, all over my body', not just the fingers.
activities.intendedInsight: Each external body part has a name, and each of the five senses is linked to a specific body part you can point to on yourself; taste is mainly the tongue and touch is the skin all over the body.

activities.title: First-hand sense play (the real anchor)
feedback: Prompt the child to name both the sense and the organ each time: 'You heard the bird — with your…? Ears!'.
If a child uses only fingertips in the feely bag, invite them to try an arm or cheek to discover skin feels everywhere.
Affirm specific, real examples the child gives rather than generic praise.
activities.rationale: Best-practice guidance is to anchor every sense to a first-hand sensory experience so the organ–sense link is embodied, not rote. Real sense-play provides the concrete experience that an on-screen figure names and labels; the two are intended to work together.
sourceClaims: Young children commonly think touch is only in the fingers and taste is in the whole mouth; anchoring senses to first-hand experiences supports accurate organ–sense mapping.
learnerActions: Smell something in a jar covered with a cloth or a lid with holes (orange, flower) using only your nose, then name the sense.
Explore a 'feely bag' of textures with your hands and also against your arm or cheek to show skin feels all over.
Go on a listening walk and name the sounds you hear with your ears.
Taste a tiny piece of food and notice what your tongue tells you.
After each activity, say which sense you used and which body part did the work.
activities.intendedInsight: The senses are real, first-hand experiences of your own body; doing them is intended to make the organ–sense link stick.

activities.title: Senses in action: sort objects by sense
feedback: When an object is placed on an unexpected sense, ask how you'd actually find out about it; accept any sense the child can justify (you can also see a bell or an ice cube), then ask which sense tells you the bell is ringing or the ice cube is cold.
Confirm correct sorts with the child restating the organ: 'Yes — you smell the cookie with your nose'.
If taste and smell are confused on a food item, note they often team up when we eat, and both are senses.
activities.rationale: Multi-sensory sorting ('which sense tells you about this?') lets the child DO the mapping and apply it to real objects with feedback. A sort of this kind can have the child apply and practise the classification and, with the added 'say a sentence' step, elicit a short explanation. Applying the mapping through doing-with-feedback is intended to reinforce the naming delivered by the labelled figure; this is a proposed approach rather than a source-established comparison against passive review.
learnerActions: Look at real objects or pictures (a bell, a cookie, an ice cube, a flower) and decide which sense tells you about each.
Drag or place each object next to the correct sense organ (bell → ears, cookie smell → nose, ice cube → skin/touch).
Drag or place name labels onto the correct parts of a body outline.
Say a short sentence for each match, e.g. 'The bell is for hearing — I use my ears'.
activities.intendedInsight: The sense→organ mapping applies to real objects and situations, not just to naming parts in isolation.

constraints: Keep everything external and observational — no internal organs, nervous system, or 'how seeing works' mechanisms at this age.

Handle two subtleties gently: the tongue is the main body part for taste (a few taste buds elsewhere in the mouth help a little, so do not tell children the rest of the mouth tastes nothing), and touch is the skin all over the body (not just fingertips).
Avoid the early misconception that eyes 'send out' something to see; if it arises, keep the response simple and do not introduce light-reception mechanisms yet.
Mention in passing that many other animals have these senses too (though not every animal has all five), so children don't assume senses are human-only.
A labelled on-screen figure names and reveals links but does not elicit real sensory handling; pair screen work with real classroom sense-play as the primary first-hand anchor.

Scored matching/multiple-choice can check the mapping but does not itself elicit the first-hand experience or explanation; best-practice anchoring is to lead with real first-hand sense-play rather than relying on a scored check alone.
Smell and taste working together is a real phenomenon, but a blocked-nose taste test should only be done safely, with familiar foods and no choking or allergy risk; keep it gentle and optional.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three sources are marked unverified in the row (NGSS mapping claim and the OU OpenLearn misconception/first-hand-experience claim); do not treat them as confirmed.
The 'eyes send out something to see' item is listed as a misconception to keep simple; the guidance deliberately avoids teaching any seeing mechanism, which is appropriate for age 5–6.
The source's blindfold/nose-pinch taste test is retained only as an optional, safely-run demonstration; ensure no allergy/choking hazard before use.

Claims that doing-with-feedback or playful reveal 'teach better' than scored tests or passive review were softened to proposed/scoped wording, as no source in the row establishes such efficacy comparisons.

The row's US/NGSS cross-standard context was condensed out of the learner guidance; the UK Y1 standard anchors the summary. Reinstate the US note only if downstream guidance needs the cross-curriculum framing.

assess.poeTask: Blindfold a child and pinch their nose shut, then have them taste small pieces of apple and raw potato (or onion). Ask them first to PREDICT whether they'll tell the foods apart by taste alone, and why. Most predict yes ('my tongue tastes it'); struggling to distinguish them with the nose blocked reveals that smell drives much of flavour.
probeDeeper: If you closed your eyes, could you still tell someone was stroking your arm — which sense is that and which body part?
When you have a cold and a blocked nose, does your dinner taste as strong? Why might that be?
Which sense would help you cross a road safely, and which body part does it use?
Can you feel with your feet or your back, or only your hands — how could we test it?
assess.correctAnswer: The nose smells the cookies and the ears hear the beep. Feeling is done by the skin, which covers the whole body — not just the fingers — so any bit of skin (an arm, a cheek) can feel warmth or touch.

errorPatterns.pattern: You feel and touch only with your fingers or hands ('you feel with your hands')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Touch a warm (safe) mug to the cheek or forearm and ask what they feel; the whole skin is the organ of touch.
errorPatterns.distractor: Only your fingers can feel whether something is hot.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says only fingers can feel whether something is hot; doesn't offer skin as the sense organ

errorPatterns.pattern: You smell with your mouth / taste with your nose (taste and smell muddled)
errorPatterns.nextMove: The nose smells and the tongue tastes; show they team up by tasting food with the nose pinched.
errorPatterns.distractor: You smell the cookies with your mouth.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assigns the wrong organ — says you smell the cookies with your mouth or taste with your nose

errorPatterns.pattern: Taste is all done by the tongue — a blocked nose wouldn't change it
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do a nose-pinched taste test; smell contributes a lot to flavour, so blocking the nose dulls taste.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says food would taste exactly the same with a blocked-up nose

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably match sense organ to sense, or thinks feeling happens only in the hands.
responseLevels.full: Matches all five senses to their organs, knows skin all over is the touch organ, and explains taste and smell work together with a real example.
responseLevels.partial: Matches the obvious organs (eyes→see, ears→hear) but muddles taste/smell or limits touch to fingers.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You walk into the kitchen and you can smell cookies baking, then the oven timer beeps and you hear it. Which part of your body did you use to smell the cookies, and which to hear the beep? And when you touch the warm tray to see if it's hot — is it only your fingers that can feel, or can other parts of you feel too?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the sense organs names nose for smell and ears for hearing and knows touch works through skin all over. A child who has only a partial picture says only the fingers can feel, or muddles taste and smell.
